caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:001603
attempts.paper_title: Preconfigured neuronal firing sequences in human brain organoids

inputs.what: The d2 code of Sooter et al. that the paper's r_download.sh fetches (myYuleWalker.m, myAutocorr.m, getFixedPointDistance.m, getAvalanches.m, getARstats.m, simAR.m), read and ported to sequences.py for supp27-d2-near-critical; no data from it are used.

attempts.entry_title: Preconfigured firing sequences in brain organoids (van der Molen et al. 2025)
attempts.summary: The paper's central findings on human organoids held in this data: bursts are organised around backbone units that fire in every burst and correlate more across bursts and with each other than non-rigid units, as in mouse cortical slices. Hidden Markov models fit the bursts better than shuffled data, but states did not converge at the burst peak in most organoids, and state features did not classify units better than firing rate. Several cross-model comparisons in Fig. 7 failed for murine organoids, where the paper does not give the burst detection used and four of nine show no bursts under the stated settings. Minor rank-order claims could not be tested, as the paper gives two conflicting normalisations.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of van der Molen, Spaeth, Chini et al. (2025) on dandiset 001603, which holds the sorted spike trains of 8 human organoids, 9 murine organoids, 6 neonatal mouse slices and 8 primary cultures, murine organoids treated with gabazine and with NBQX and R-CPP, and longitudinal human organoid recordings. It detects population bursts and backbone units, and compares burst-to-burst and pairwise correlations, burst similarity, PCA, d2 and hidden Markov models between unit groups and model types.

notebooks.title: Bursts, backbone units, correlations and model comparisons (Figs. 1 to 4, 6 and 7)
Hidden Markov models (Figs. 5 and 7F, Supplementary Figs. 18, 24D and 26)

outcomes.statement: The analysed segment of each recording holds about 40 population bursts (38 ± 4, mean ± SE).
outcomes.source: Methods, Comparing data from different sources
outcomes.quote: The recording durations per data source were selected so that each recording contained around 40 bursts (38 ± 4 bursts, mean ± SE)
outcomes.notes: Mean 34.8 bursts over the 31 recordings under the code's lengths (SE 6.3, range 0 to 156), within 38 plus or minus 4. The mean matches but the recordings do not each hold about 40 bursts; four murine organoids (MO2, MO4, MO5, MO6) have none under the stated detection and MO1 and MO7 have 113 and 156, which offset them. With 800 ms minimum distance the mean is 34.7; with 2000 ms for every recording it is 29.5, outside, but the Methods raise the distance only for recordings with long bursts. 35 overlapping bursts in 13 recordings are dropped (none in HO1 to HO4).
deviations: Matlab smoothdata replaced by scipy filters (moving mean; Gaussian with standard deviation one fifth of the window, cut at the window), a standard choice.

Of overlapping bursts (a peak in the tail of a longer burst), only the one with the higher peak is kept, at 700 ms in every recording. The Methods raise min_dist "up to 2000 ms" for "recordings with long duration bursts ... to prevent peaks in the tail of the burst from being detected as separate burst instances" without naming the recordings; this applies the stated purpose to all (35 bursts in 13 recordings). 2000 ms for every recording is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: In the example human organoid of Figs. 1 and 2, 46 bursts occur in a three-minute interval.
outcomes.source: Figure 1C legend; Figure 2C legend
outcomes.quote: The population firing rate (gray lines) is plotted relative to the burst peak for 46 burst events measured across a three-minute interval for the same organoid
outcomes.notes: HO1 has 46 bursts in its first 180 s with 700 ms and with 800 ms minimum peak distance (HO2 to HO4 have 31, 42 and 28). HO1 is the example organoid for the dependent claims.

outcomes.statement: In each of the 8 human organoids the distribution of unit mean firing rates is well fit by a lognormal distribution (R² 0.97 ± 0.04, mean ± STD), while the rates of backbone units alone are not (R² 0.45 ± 0.30).
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 1A to C
outcomes.quote: we observed that the distribution of firing rates follows a heavy-tailed, right-skewed lognormal distribution ( n = 8, R 2 = 0.97 ± 0.04, Extended Data Fig. 1A – C ) ... Backbone neurons alone are not well described by a lognormal distribution. R 2 values are 0.45±0.30 across the 8 human brain organoids
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a) with all sorted units (the code's choice) the mean R squared is 0.949 for all units and 0.487 for backbone units (seven organoids; HO7 has no backbone unit), both within tolerance. The code's form of the density gives 0.944 and 0.442. With units of at least 30 spikes the all-unit mean is 0.919, outside. Reading (b), the legend's normal fit to log rates, gives 0.60 and 0.36.
deviations: The fit follows plot_multi_rec_figs_backbone.m (two-parameter density, start values 1 and 0.25, bins up to the last non-empty one), read from the paper's code at e9a79c4.

outcomes.statement: Burst durations in the human organoids are on the order of 10² ms.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 1; Figure 1D; Supplementary Fig. 1C
outcomes.quote: Bursts exhibited consistent rate profiles within organoids ( Fig. 1C ), with durations spanning timescales on the order of ≈ 10 2 milliseconds ( Fig. 1D , Supplementary Fig. 1 C )
outcomes.notes: Median burst durations of HO1 to HO4 are 511, 628, 472 and 891.5 ms, all between 100 and 1000 ms. Over the 27 recordings with bursts the medians run from 104 ms (Pr4) to 2681 ms (MO3); HO6, MO3 and MO9 are above 1000 ms.

outcomes.statement: Most units reach their peak firing rate close to the peak of the population burst.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 1; Figure 1E
outcomes.quote: A majority of units firing rates peaked in close proximity to the population burst maxima ( Fig. 1E )
outcomes.notes: More than half of the values fall within the bound in 15 of 16 combinations of organoid, quantity and bound (fractions 0.53 to 0.89). The exception is HO4, pooled unit-burst peak times within 50 ms (0.481). The criterion names the readings and requires every one, and defines no partial outcome; the effect is present and falls short in one reading of one organoid, so the claim holds in part (the rule for partial outcomes is in the notebook's summary).

outcomes.statement: Backbone units, which fire at least twice in every burst, are 28% ± 14% (mean ± STD) of the units in the 8 human organoids.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 3; Supplementary Fig. 1A
outcomes.quote: Backbone units, comprising 28% ± 14% (mean ± STD) of total neurons ( n = 8 organoids, Supplementary Fig. 1 )
outcomes.notes: With units of at least 30 spikes as the denominator (reading b), mean 0.331 and SD 0.150, both within tolerance. With all sorted units, mean 0.258 (within) and SD 0.166 (outside 0.126 to 0.154). HO7 has no backbone unit here (no unit fires twice in all 21 bursts); HO1 to HO4 have 27, 26, 23 and 15.

outcomes.statement: Backbone units have higher burst-to-burst correlations of their firing rate than non-rigid units.
outcomes.source: Figure 2E legend; Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Backbone neurons consistently exhibited higher burst-to-burst correlation coefficients compared to non-rigid units ( P < 10 −16 , two-sided linear mixed-effects model, n = 4 organoids and 507 single-units)
outcomes.notes: Backbone 0.796 against non-rigid 0.574 (effect 0.210, p 3e-27, 216 units) under the Methods' 30% rule, and 0.796 against 0.629 (p 9e-16, 150 units) under the code's 70% rule; higher in each organoid. The measured value is the number of sorted units in HO1 to HO4, which equals the paper's n of 507; the units that pass the unit rules and enter the test are 216 or 150. Burst-to-burst correlations exist only for units active in bursts, so a test over all 507 units cannot be run.
deviations: Burst-only rates do not hold the inverse ISI across the gap between bursts (the code does, giving rates below 1 Hz between bursts).

Mixed models fitted by REML with a random intercept, tested with t on Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (sequences.lmm, checked against an exact balanced case), in place of the paper's R; the 30-spike rule counts spikes over the whole analysed recording.

outcomes.statement: Among backbone units, the variance of firing-rate peak times across bursts grows with the unit's position in the sequence, so later-firing units are more variable.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 3; Figure 2F and 2G
outcomes.quote: Finally, the variability of firing peak times increased with their average latency ( Fig. 2F ), a relationship consistently observed across organoids ( Fig. 2G , P < 10 −5 , linear mixed-effects model)

statistics.about: Figure 2G legend, relation between relative firing rate peak and peak time variance

outcomes.notes: Over 91 backbone units the peak-time variance rises with relative position, p 6e-4 for the rank reading and 1e-4 for the rescaled median time (log variance, p 3e-6 and 1e-6); the rank correlation is positive in each organoid (0.11 to 0.68).

outcomes.statement: When bursts are clustered by their pairwise unit correlation matrices, the firing rates of non-rigid units vary more between clusters than those of backbone units.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 3F
outcomes.quote: Clustering bursts by their pairwise correlation matrix confirmed that backbone patterns were preserved across clusters, whereas non-rigid units varied substantially ( P < 10 −20 , linear mixed-effects model; Extended Data Fig. 3 )
outcomes.notes: Non-rigid units vary more between burst clusters than backbone units under both elbow readings and both organoid sets (mean CV 0.64 to 1.31 against 0.07 to 0.30; p 6e-40 to 2e-84). The kneedle rule picks 3 to 7 clusters, the silhouette 2 or 3.
deviations: k from 2 to 10 with 10 k-means++ seeds per k (the code's range of k is a parameter not given).

outcomes.statement: In murine organoids, blocking GABA-A receptors with gabazine increases the number of population bursts.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 4B
outcomes.quote: Meanwhile, the number of bursts increase after gabazine treatment ( P < 0.05, two-sided linear mixed-effect model)
outcomes.notes: Burst rate rises with gabazine in each of the four organoids with a baseline (by 2.7 to 10.6 bursts per minute); mixed model 7.1 per minute, p 0.011 (5 organoids, 9 recordings); paired t-test over the four, p 0.021.
deviations: MO12 has no baseline sorted file; its gabazine recording enters the mixed model only.

outcomes.statement: Blocking AMPA and NMDA receptors with NBQX and R-CPP abolishes population bursts in murine organoids.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 4B
outcomes.quote: Note that bursting disappears after NBQX and R-CPP treatment reflected as a significant decrease in bursting compared to baseline conditions ( P < 0.001, two-sided linear mixed-effect model)
outcomes.notes: The five NBQX with R-CPP recordings have 0, 0, 1 (MO12), 0 and 0 bursts against 81 to 114 at baseline; burst rate falls by 10.1 per minute, p 9e-7.

outcomes.statement: Gabazine increases the fraction of bursts in which units fire at least two spikes.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 4C
outcomes.quote: The fraction of bursts in which units are active increases significantly after gabazine treatment ( P < 10 −7 , two-sided linear mixed-effect model)
outcomes.notes: Units pooled per condition (the dataset does not identify units across recordings), the fraction of bursts with at least two spikes rises by 0.139 with gabazine, p 9e-4, in each of the four organoids with a baseline. Treating units as matched in MO10, MO11 and MO14, whose unit positions are identical across conditions, gives 0.152, p 7e-8; MO12 has no baseline file and MO13's positions differ between conditions, so both are left out of that variant.

outcomes.statement: Gabazine makes the order of backbone sequences more consistent across bursts.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 4D
outcomes.quote: There is a significant increase in backbone sequence order similarity after treatment with gabazine ( P < 10 −20 , two-sided linear mixed-effect model)
outcomes.notes: The criterion requires gabazine to be higher with p < 0.05 under both normalisation readings, and they disagree. Raw rank-order correlations of backbone sequences rise with gabazine in every organoid (medians 0.07 to 0.35 at baseline, 0.55 to 0.91 with gabazine; 0.381, p printed as 0), and z-scored to the shuffles, as the Extended Data Fig. 4D legend says, gabazine is higher by 2.0 (p printed as 0). As (A - B)/(A + B) per burst pair, the Supplementary Methods' normalisation for this measure, it is not (-1.15, p 0.6). Per burst pair the ratio is unstable (the shuffled Spearman correlations are centred on 0, median 0.009, so A + B changes sign for 8.8% of burst pairs and the ratio runs from -86,000 to 3,200), but its per-recording medians are stable (0.855 to 0.996) and rise with gabazine in MO10, MO11 and MO13 and fall slightly in MO14 (0.959 to 0.953). Recorded as reproduced on the assumed z-score after round 1, and changed to blocked in round 3 with the verifier's agreement. Which normalisation was used, and at which level, is asked of the authors (methods_unavailable finding).
deviations: The rank-order correlations are normalised both by z-score to the shuffles, as the Extended Data Fig. 4D legend says, and as (A - B)/(A + B), the Supplementary Methods' normalisation, which is unstable on signed correlations whose shuffle mean is near 0.

outcomes.statement: The fraction of backbone units declines as human and murine organoids mature.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 2; Supplementary Fig. 2A
outcomes.quote: Longitudinal recordings showed that the relative fraction of backbone units declined over development ( Supplementary Fig. 2 )
outcomes.notes: In HO2 and HO3 the backbone fraction is lower at 8 months than at 6 months on average and in each organoid, with either denominator (all units 0.31 and 0.37 to 0.11 and 0.11). The murine part cannot be tested, as the dandiset holds no longitudinal murine organoid recordings (all MO files are P45D).

outcomes.statement: The burst-to-burst correlation of units increases over development in human and murine organoids, and backbone units are higher than non-rigid units at every age.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 3; Supplementary Fig. 2C
outcomes.quote: Their firing patterns remained stable across hours ( Supplementary Fig. 8 ) and persisted over months, with correlations increasing during development in both human and murine organoids ( Supplementary Fig. 2C , P < 10 −5 , two-way ANOVA)
outcomes.notes: In HO2 and HO3 the burst-to-burst correlation rises with age (0.61, 0.69, 0.72 at 6, 7 and 8 months; age effect F 18.7, p 2e-8 with unit type as the second factor, F 13.3, p 3e-6 with organoid), and backbone units are above non-rigid units at every age. The murine part cannot be tested (no longitudinal murine organoid recordings).

outcomes.statement: Units classed as backbone in one recording are mostly classed as backbone again 4 h later, units classed as non-rigid are mostly classed as non-rigid again, and backbone units keep more consistent firing patterns across the two recordings than non-rigid units.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 8A and 8E
outcomes.quote: the majority of units that was detected as a backbone unit at time point 0-hour was also detected as backbone unit at time point 4-hour (top left) for both organoids. Meanwhile, the majority of units that were detected as non-rigid units at time point 0-hour were also detected as non-rigid units at time point 4-hour (bottom right) for both organoids
outcomes.notes: Units linked by position, walking both units tables in order. All 90 HO2 units and all 116 HO3 units at 0 h are linked; the two ordered lists of positions are identical, apart from one extra 4 h unit in HO3 (unit 24). Of the 0 h backbone units, 8 of 10 (HO2) and 13 of 13 (HO3) are backbone at 4 h; of the non-rigid units, 74 of 80 and 97 of 103 stay non-rigid. Across recordings, backbone units have higher burst-to-burst correlations than non-rigid units in both organoids (HO2 0.748 against 0.627, Welch p 0.039; HO3 0.820 against 0.607, p 4e-8, 30% rule); with the 70% rule the means are still higher (HO2 0.738 against 0.699, p 0.62; HO3 p 0.001). Within each recording alone backbone units are above non-rigid units too.
deviations: Assumption. The dandiset has no unit identifier across the 0 h and 4 h recordings. Units are linked by their identical (x, y) positions in the same order, which joint sorting gives and two separate sortings would not; positions alone are not unique (61 distinct positions for 90 HO2 units). Results of each recording alone are also shown.

Cross-recording burst-to-burst correlation, every 0 h burst against every 4 h burst in which the unit fires at least twice in the -250 to 500 ms window (Methods' burst-to-burst correlation, bursts paired across recordings as Supplementary Fig. 8E), units passing the unit rules in both recordings.

outcomes.statement: Randomizing spike times while keeping unit and population rates reduces burst-to-burst correlations.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal dynamics of neuronal firing sequences, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 5D; Supplementary Fig. 9A
outcomes.quote: Randomized spike trains that preserved mean and single-unit firing rates abolished sequences and significantly reduced burst-to-bust correlations ( Extended Data Fig. 5 , Supplementary Figs. 9 - 10 )
outcomes.notes: Backbone units of HO1 to HO8 (259 with both values), real 0.605 against shuffled mean 0.492; (a) 0.112 with a random intercept per organoid, p 1e-26, per unit p 2e-28; (b) normalised mean 0.082, one-sided p 0.014. HO8 goes the other way (-0.034).
deviations: 10 shuffles per recording, where the paper uses 100. Reading (a) fits the unit and organoid intercepts one at a time, where the criterion names both together.

outcomes.statement: Pairwise cross-correlations of firing rates are higher between backbone units than between backbone and non-rigid units or between non-rigid units.
outcomes.source: Figure 3E legend; Results, Backbone units are a highly correlated ensemble
outcomes.quote: Correlations between backbone units (blue) are significantly higher ( P < 10 −20 , 2-sided linear mixed effects model, n = 4 organoids and 34,056 single unit pairs) than the cross-correlations between pairs of backbone and non-rigid units (gray) and pairs of non-rigid units (yellow)
outcomes.notes: Backbone pairs 0.70 against mixed 0.36 and non-rigid 0.23, both contrasts p printed as 0, in each organoid. The measured value is the number of pairs among all sorted units of HO1 to HO4, which equals the paper's n; 9,648 pairs among units with at least 30 spikes enter the test.

outcomes.statement: The distribution of pairwise correlations is skewed and roughly lognormal, and backbone-backbone pairs lie in its upper tail in every organoid.
outcomes.source: Figure 3F legend; Results, Backbone units are a highly correlated ensemble
outcomes.quote: The histogram of all pairwise cross-correlations follows a skewed, lognormal distribution ( x -axis is log scale). The pairwise connections between pairs of backbone units populate the tail of this distribution for all organoids
outcomes.notes: The backbone-pair mean lies above the 75th percentile of all pairs in every organoid (87th to 95th percentile) and above the 90th in three of four (HO3 at the 87th). The criterion requires both readings and defines no partial outcome; the effect is present and falls short at the 90th percentile in one organoid, so the claim holds in part (the rule for partial outcomes is in the notebook's summary). Skew 0.26 to 1.08; R squared of a normal fit to the log correlations 0.28 to 0.80.

outcomes.statement: The spread of burst similarity across pairs of bursts is high outside bursts, drops at burst onset and stays low until the bursts end.
outcomes.source: Results, Population firing rate timing across burst epochs, paragraph 1; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: Variance in similarity showed the opposite trend: it was high during non-bursting periods, rapidly declining at burst onset, and remaining low until bursts ended ( Fig. 4C )
outcomes.notes: In HO1 the standard deviation of similarity over burst pairs is 0.142 inside against 0.191 outside (median burst edges) and 0.133 against 0.163 (backbone window); lower inside in every organoid.

outcomes.statement: Across pairs of bursts, the population firing vectors of backbone units are more similar (cosine similarity) throughout the backbone window than those of non-rigid units or of shuffled data.
outcomes.source: Figure 4D legend; Results, Population firing rate timing across burst epochs, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Backbone units consistently display significantly higher similarity throughout the backbone window compared with non-rigid or shuffled controls ( P < 10 −20 , paired two-sided t-test)
outcomes.notes: In HO1 backbone similarity exceeds non-rigid and shuffled similarity significantly at all 226 frames of the backbone window (Bonferroni). The same in HO2 to HO6; HO8 67% and 45% of frames.
deviations: Shuffled similarity averaged over 3 shuffles, where the paper uses 100.

outcomes.statement: In every human organoid the burst similarity rises from the onset of the backbone period and stays high during it.
outcomes.source: Results, Population firing rate timing across burst epochs, paragraph 1; Figure 4E; Supplementary Fig. 13D
outcomes.quote: Across organoids, burst similarity increased at backbone onset and plateaued during their activation ( Fig. 4E , Supplementary Fig. 13D , n = 8 organoids)
outcomes.notes: In the seven organoids with backbone units the mean similarity over the backbone period exceeds its value at the first frame (HO8 barely, 0.334 against 0.323). HO7 has no backbone unit under the 100% rule, so no backbone period; 7 of 8.

outcomes.statement: The 20% of units with the highest average pairwise correlation give a higher burst similarity than all units together, and the 20% with the lowest give a lower one.
outcomes.source: Results, Population firing rate timing across burst epochs, paragraph 1; Supplementary Fig. 13A to C
outcomes.quote: Notably, the top 20th percentile of highly correlated units (from Fig. 3C ) generated significantly higher burst similarity than the full population, with the effect diminishing as larger percentiles were included ( Supplementary Fig. 13A , C ). Conversely, the lowest 20th percentile reduced similarity
outcomes.notes: In HO1 the top 20% (19 units) give similarity 0.868 and the bottom 20% 0.056 against 0.453 for all units, each significant at every frame of the window. Top minus bottom summed similarity falls from 183.6 at 20% to 6.3 at 95%.

outcomes.statement: In the example organoid, the first two principal components of backbone unit rates explain 73% of their variance against 25% for non-rigid units, and across organoids backbone units need fewer components than all units while non-rigid units need more.
outcomes.source: Results, Population firing rate timing across burst epochs, paragraph 2; Figure 4F and 4G; Supplementary Fig. 14
outcomes.quote: When populations were divided, backbone units captured far more variance (73%) in the first two PCs compared to non-rigid units (25%) ( Fig. 4F middle/right, Fig. 4G , Supplementary Figs. 14 - 15 )
outcomes.notes: In HO1 the first two PCs explain 75.4% for backbone units (within 73 plus or minus 7.3) and 17.4% for non-rigid units (outside 25 plus or minus 2.5); no organoid matches both. With the code's burst-only rates, which hold the inverse ISI across the gaps between bursts, HO1 gives 75.1% and 15.3%, again no organoid matches both. In each of the seven organoids with backbone units, backbone is above and non-rigid below all units; HO7 has no backbone unit.

outcomes.statement: Hidden Markov models fitted to the organoid spike trains give a higher held-out log likelihood on real data than on randomized data with the same unit and population rates.
outcomes.source: Results, Revealing temporal structure with a hidden Markov model, paragraph 1; Supplementary Fig. 18
outcomes.quote: Log likelihood is always greater for real than for randomized data, with no overlap between the distributions for real and shuffled data
outcomes.notes: Held-out log likelihood per entry, scored on both as log p(held-out | rest), is higher on real data than on the surrogate in all 120 fold, K and organoid combinations with 20% held out (smallest margin 0.015 nats per entry, HO4 at K 30; every fold's margin printed) and in all 40 with 10% held out (smallest 0.021). The round-1 scoring gave the surrogate the marginal likelihood of its held-out entries, 0.008 nats per entry lower on average; with it the smallest margin was 0.009.
deviations: HMMs fitted with the entry's EM (hmm.py) in place of SSM; K = 10, 20 and 30 for the cross-validation; folds refitted from scratch; entries held out at random, at 20% (Supplementary Methods) and 10% (the code).

outcomes.statement: The diversity of HMM states is high before and after bursts and reaches a minimum near the burst peak, where states follow a stereotyped path.
outcomes.source: Results, Revealing temporal structure with a hidden Markov model, paragraph 2; Figure 5C; Supplementary Fig. 19B
outcomes.quote: Notably, entropy consistently approaches a local minimum near burst peaks, indicating a convergence toward specific states with higher transition probabilities during the initiation of sequential activation patterns
outcomes.notes: The state entropy across bursts (averaged over K) has its minimum below both window ends in seven organoids, within 90 ms of the peak in one (HO8), and within the backbone window in three (HO1, HO6, HO8); in HO2, HO3 and HO4 it lies 120 to 510 ms before the peak, where in HO3 and HO4 the entropy is already near 0 at the window's start (0.015 and 0.18). The criterion needs 6 of 8 under both readings.
deviations: K = 10, 12, ..., 30 (11 models per recording) in place of every K from 10 to 30, at most 300 EM iterations (41 of 341 models stopped there), with the entry's EM in place of SSM.

outcomes.statement: Backbone units are active across a larger pool of HMM states than non-rigid units.
outcomes.source: Results, Revealing temporal structure with a hidden Markov model, paragraph 3; Figure 5D; Supplementary Fig. 21
outcomes.quote: Backbone ensembles spanned a larger pool of HMM states than non-rigid units ( Fig. 5D , Supplementary Fig. 21 )
outcomes.notes: Backbone units are consistent in more states (by 3.7) and have higher mean consistency (by 0.17) than non-rigid units, p printed as 0 for both, over 7 organoids and 11 K; higher in each organoid. HO7 has no backbone unit.
deviations: K enters as a fixed factor, where the criterion names a random intercept for K.

outcomes.statement: A linear classifier on HMM state consistency separates backbone from non-rigid units with 83.9% ± 12.0% accuracy, above the 63.2% ± 10.4% reached with firing rate alone.
outcomes.source: Results, Revealing temporal structure with a hidden Markov model, paragraph 3; Figure 5F
outcomes.quote: Linear support vector machine classifiers trained on hidden state features distinguished backbone from non-rigid units with 83.9% ± 12.0% accuracy, significantly exceeding the 63.2% ± 10.4% achieved when using firing rate alone ( Fig. 5F )
outcomes.notes: State-feature accuracy 86.5% plus or minus 11.6 over all models is within 83.9 plus or minus 12.0; rate accuracy 73.9% plus or minus 23.2 over seven organoids is outside 63.2 plus or minus 10.4. States beat rate in neither test, (a) paired over organoids p 0.086, (b) per organoid significant in four of seven; in HO2, HO3 and HO4 rate alone reaches 89% to 95%. The majority class is 54% to 88% of units (mean 70.6%); rate-only accuracy is below it in HO5 and HO8. The paper states no chance level. HO7 has no backbone unit to classify. The criterion defines no partial outcome, and its central comparison, states against rate, fails under both readings, so the claim is not reproduced (the rule for partial outcomes is in the notebook's summary).

outcomes.statement: In neonatal mouse cortical slices, backbone units have higher burst-to-burst correlations than non-rigid units.
outcomes.source: Figure 6F legend; Results, Endogenous sequences in early developing neonatal cortex, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Backbone units consistently exhibited higher correlations than non-rigid units (P < 10 −20 , two-sided linear mixed-effects model, n = 6 mice and 959 single units)
outcomes.notes: Backbone units have higher correlations at both thresholds and with a random intercept per slice or per animal (effects 0.122 to 0.159, p 5e-17 to 2e-37; 685 units in the test), and under the second reading of the recording length (p below 1e-33). The measured value is the number of sorted units in the six slices, which equals the paper's n.

outcomes.statement: In neonatal slices, backbone-backbone pairs are more strongly correlated than mixed or non-rigid pairs.
outcomes.source: Figure 6G legend
outcomes.quote: Backbone–backbone correlations were significantly stronger than mixed or non-rigid pairs (P < 10 −20 , two-sided linear mixed-effects model, n = 6 mice and 125607 single unit pairs)

statistics.n: 6 mice (six slices) and 125607 single unit pairs

outcomes.notes: Backbone pairs exceed mixed and non-rigid pairs under every reading, both recording lengths included (contrasts 0.16 to 0.26, p printed as 0; 89,669 pairs among units with at least 30 spikes). The measured value is the number of pairs among all sorted units of the slices, which equals the paper's n.

outcomes.statement: Backbone units fire at higher rates than non-rigid units in every model type (human and murine organoids, neonatal slices and primary cultures).
outcomes.source: Results, Comparing sequences across neurodevelopmental models, paragraph 1; Figure 7A
outcomes.quote: Backbone neurons had significantly higher firing rates than non-rigid counterparts ( Fig. 7A , P < 10 −6 , linear mixed-effects model, Supplementary Fig. 23 )

statistics.about: Figure 7A legend, backbone against non-rigid within each model type
statistics.test: two-sided linear mixed-effects model with interactions for unit type and model type
statistics.n: human organoids 8 (1048 units), murine organoids 9 (1179 units), slices 6 (786 units), primary cultures 8 (1048 units)

outcomes.notes: Backbone units fire faster in every model type (log10 differences 0.34 to 0.81, p below 1e-28) at both slice thresholds and both recording lengths. Unit counts with at least 30 spikes (699, 624, 813, 1744) are outside the legend's (1048, 1179, 786, 1048); all sorted units are 930, 1273, 959 and 2001, so the dandiset holds fewer human organoid units than the legend counts. The four murine organoids without bursts are left out, so murine organoids are 5 of 9 recordings.

outcomes.statement: Primary cultures fire at higher rates than organoids and neonatal slices, in both unit groups.
outcomes.source: Results, Comparing sequences across neurodevelopmental models, paragraph 1; Figure 7A

The numbers passing the AR fit check differ from the paper's 3, 7, 4 and 7 (HO, MO, MS, PR): 0, 5, 0 and 1 when every log-binned density and spectrum ratio must be within one order of magnitude (measured), 7, 9, 3 and 8 when their median must be. Assumption. The AR fit check is read as the largest (i) or the median (ii) absolute log10 ratio between the data's and a simulated AR series' avalanche size and duration densities (15 logarithmic bins, avalanche threshold at the 10% quantile as test.m) and Welch spectra (30 s segments; the code's 200 s window is longer than the 180 s recordings), at most 1. The paper says only that preparations were excluded when the distributions deviated by more than one order of magnitude.

findings.statement: The baseline sorted recording of murine organoid MO12 is not in the dandiset (its gabazine and NBQX with R-CPP sorted files are), and no longitudinal murine organoid recording (Supplementary Fig. 2) is in it; every MO file has age P45D.

Units have positions but no identifier linking them across recordings of one organoid (0 h and 4 h, Supplementary Fig. 8; drug conditions, Extended Data Fig. 4). The ordered unit positions are identical for HO2 at 0 h and 4 h (90 units), for HO3 once the 4 h file's unit 24 is left out (116 units), and for MO10, MO11 and MO14 between baseline and gabazine, which is consistent with joint sorting, but not for MO13, nor between the NBQX with R-CPP recording and any other condition of an organoid (printed with ed4c-gabazine-participation). Positions alone are not unique (61 distinct positions for 90 HO2 units).

The HO2 and HO3 recordings at 6, 7, 8 months and 8 months plus 4 h are each deposited twice under different session names, and the 7-month ones a third time as HO2_sorted.mat and HO3_sorted.mat, with identical spike matrices.

The dandiset description says only spike-sorted data are included for the sourced human organoids, but raw ecephys files are present for HO1 to HO4 (sixteen files). The slice files say "Sorting/curation not specified".

disagreements.reason: The criterion requires gabazine to be higher "under both readings". Under the ratio reading it is not (-1.15, p 0.6; cell 51). The claims file reads the paper correctly here: the Supplementary Methods name (A-B)/(A+B) for exactly this measure, while the Extended Data Fig. 4D legend says z-scored. The case for dropping the ratio reading holds only for a mean-based model on ratios computed per burst pair. Per-recording medians of the ratio are stable (0.855 to 0.996); they rise in three organoids and fall in one (MO14, 0.959 to 0.953), so the ratio reading has not been shown to carry no information. Under the claims file this should be blocked as methods_underspecified. The record says "As the verifier finds the ratio reading gives no information, the legend's z-score is adopted"; I called the ratio reading degenerate, but I concluded blocked, and did not say the z-score should be adopted.

It rests on two assumptions, and neither is consistent with the claims file. The ratio reading fails under both recording lengths (p 0.66/0.49 and 0.69/0.38; cell 129). The z reading passes under length (a) only (p 0.032/0.031). Under (b) it fails (0.064/0.099). The claims file says both lengths "are run where the outcome could depend on it", and that disagreeing readings make a claim methods_underspecified. The outcome should be blocked as methods_underspecified, not reproduced.

paper_notes.statement: Burst detection parameters for the murine organoids are not given. With the stated detection (4 x RMS of the 20 ms and 100 ms smoothed population rate) MO2, MO4, MO5 and MO6 have no burst and MO3 has four: their highest peaks reach only 3.0 to 3.7 times the RMS, because their rate between bursts is high (median smoothed population rate 0.47 to 1.07 spikes per ms), yet the paper's code lists backbone units for all nine. MO3's four bursts make 160 of its 234 units backbone units; without MO3 the murine organoid contrast of Fig. 7B holds and the murine organoid against slice lag contrast of Fig. 7D is not significant. Question for the authors, which threshold, peak distance and recording length were used for each murine organoid, and for which recordings the minimum peak distance was raised towards 2000 ms (35 overlapping bursts in 13 recordings here, a peak in the tail of a longer burst, are merged in its place).

Question for the authors on the rank-order normalisation (Extended Data Fig. 4D and Supplementary Fig. 10B). The legend says z-scored and the Supplementary Methods say (A - B)/(A + B); per burst pair, shuffled Spearman correlations average near 0, so the ratio is unstable and the two give opposite conclusions here. Which was used, and was it applied per burst pair or per recording?

The n reported with several tests counts all sorted units or pairs (507 units and 34,056 pairs in HO1 to HO4, 959 units and 125,607 pairs in the slices), while the Methods and legends restrict the tests to units with at least 30 spikes or units active in enough bursts. The Fig. 7A legend's unit counts (1048, 1179, 786, 1048) match neither all units (930, 1273, 959, 2001) nor units with at least 30 spikes here.
Pr1 to Pr4 are cultures from E18 Wistar rat cortex (Methods; the files say Rattus norvegicus), while the paper calls all primary cultures murine.

Question for the authors on the AR fit check of the d2 analysis (Supplementary Methods, d2 calculation; Supplementary Fig. 27). Preparations were excluded when the AR model's avalanche size and duration distributions or power spectrum deviated from the data's by more than one order of magnitude, but the comparison is not given (which bins, the largest or a typical deviation, the spectral window; the code's 200 s Welch window is longer than the 180 s recordings). Two readings here keep 0, 5, 0 and 1 or 7, 9, 3 and 8 recordings of HO, MO, MS and PR, against the paper's 3, 7, 4 and 7.

entries.name: van-der-molen-2025
entries.title: Preconfigured firing sequences in brain organoids (van der Molen et al. 2025)
entries.description: Tests the findings of van der Molen, Spaeth, Chini et al. (2025) on dandiset 001603, which holds the sorted spike trains of 8 human organoids, 9 murine organoids, 6 neonatal mouse slices and 8 primary cultures, murine organoids treated with gabazine and with NBQX and R-CPP, and longitudinal human organoid recordings. It detects population bursts and backbone units, and compares burst-to-burst and pairwise correlations, burst similarity, PCA, d2 and hidden Markov models between unit groups and model types.

notebooks.title: Bursts, backbone units, correlations and model comparisons (Figs. 1 to 4, 6 and 7)
Hidden Markov models (Figs. 5 and 7F, Supplementary Figs. 18, 24D and 26)
